one_liner: Header-only C++20 graph library positioned as a lighter Boost.Graph alternative; measured slower than Boost.Graph on every benchmarked algorithm.
what_it_does: Graaf provides directed_graph<V, E> and undirected_graph<V, E> containers that hold arbitrary user vertex and edge payloads, plus free-function algorithms in graaf::algorithm (BFS/DFS, Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, A*, Kruskal, Prim, Tarjan/Kosaraju SCC, Kahn and DFS topological sort, greedy and Welsh-Powell colouring, Bron-Kerbosch, PageRank) and DOT export. The graph assigns vertex ids itself (add_vertex returns the id; ids freed by remove_vertex are reused). It is not a drop-in for Boost.Graph: there are no property maps, visitors or graph concepts, and algorithms return std::unordered_map/std::vector/tree results instead of filling caller-supplied maps.
how_it_is_fast: It is not faster than its named baseline. Since September 2026 the graph keeps vertices and neighbour lists in dense std::vector storage indexed by vertex id (PRs #434, #438, #442, #446) and the algorithms replaced unordered_map/unordered_set bookkeeping with lazily grown vectors (BFS uses vector<bool>, Kruskal a vector-backed union-find with union by rank and path compression, Prim and Dijkstra binary heaps with lazy deletion). Edge payloads still live in one std::unordered_map keyed by the (sorted) vertex pair, so every weighted relaxation does a hash lookup (open issue #444), and dijkstra_shortest_paths materialises a std::list path for every reachable vertex, which is where most of its 7-17x gap comes from.
when_to_use: Small to medium graphs (thousands to low hundreds of thousands of edges) where readable code and user-defined vertex/edge structs matter more than raw speed.
Teaching, prototyping or tooling where you want a one-include, dependency-free C++20 library with DOT output instead of Boost's property-map and visitor machinery.
Code that needs the full path to every vertex from Dijkstra or A* returned as a ready-made container rather than reconstructed from a predecessor map.
Projects that cannot take a Boost dependency but need the common textbook algorithms (MST, SCC, topological sort, colouring, cliques, PageRank).
when_not_to_use: Any throughput-sensitive workload: on SNAP web-Google and web-BerkStan the project's own numbers put it 1.14x (Kruskal) to 17.01x (all-targets Dijkstra) slower than Boost.Graph 1.84 adjacency_list<vecS, vecS, undirectedS>.

Large weighted graphs: every edge-weight read goes through an unordered_map<pair, edge_t> lookup, and dijkstra_shortest_paths returns a std::list per reachable vertex, so memory grows with the sum of all path lengths.

When you need Boost.Graph features such as property maps, visitors, max-flow, isomorphism, betweenness or articulation points (max-flow, articulation points, centrality and isomorphism are open feature issues #331, #332, #337, #338).
Concurrent use: thread-safety guarantees are undocumented (issue #323, marked stale), and CI covers Linux only (Windows/macOS CI is open issue #322).
If you need a stable, released version of the faster code: the September 2026 vector-storage work is unreleased (latest release v1.2.0 of 12 Sep 2026, 186 commits behind main).

integration.dependencies: none for the library (fmt was removed in #305); the perf/ and test/ builds fetch Google Benchmark v1.8.2, fmt 9.1.0, GoogleTest and, opt-in, Boost 1.84.0
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (CMakeLists sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20; CI tests g++-12 and clang++-16; v1.2.0 notes include fixes for gcc-14 and gcc 16 / clang 23 includes)
integration.platforms: any platform with a C++20 compiler in principle; CI is Linux only
integration.thread_safety: not documented (issue #323 'Document thread-safety guarantees' is open and stale); algorithms take the graph by const reference and allocate their own state

gotchas: Harness flaw in the Boost single-pair Dijkstra benchmark (PR #453 numbers): perf/boost/utils/farthest_vertex.cpp picks std::max_element over Boost's distance map, but the Boost graph is pre-sized to max dataset id + 1 and unreachable vertices keep distance std::numeric_limits<int>::max(), so the chosen 'farthest' target is an unreachable vertex; the stop_at_target_visitor never fires and Boost always runs a full single-source Dijkstra, while Graaf (whose dijkstra_shortest_paths map only holds reachable vertices) stops at the true farthest vertex. The bias works against Boost, so the 4.38x / 12.56x gap is if anything understated; the shared-source perf/common code otherwise builds identical edge lists for both libraries. A smaller bias the other way: the Boost Welsh-Powell benchmark re-sorts one persistent order vector inside the timed loop, so after the first iteration it sorts already-sorted input.

The full-graph BFS and Dijkstra benchmarks pass start vertex 1 to both libraries, but the Boost reader uses raw dataset ids while the Graaf reader remaps ids in first-seen order, so Graaf's vertex 1 is the second distinct id in the file, not dataset node 1; both very probably sit in the giant component (855,802 of 875,713 vertices in web-Google, 654,782 of 685,230 in web-BerkStan per the repo's own comment), so the effect should be small. The Prim benchmark avoids this by remapping inside perf/common/connected_subgraph.h, and its comment ('re-scans every fringe vertex's neighbor list') is stale since #387 switched Prim to a binary heap, which is why it still runs on capped 85,000/80,000-vertex subgraphs.

add_edge throws std::invalid_argument when either vertex is missing or when the edge already exists (update in place via get_edge instead); dijkstra throws on a negative edge weight; prim_minimum_spanning_tree returns std::nullopt for a disconnected graph instead of a spanning forest.

README installs from the release page, which ships v1.2.0 without the September 2026 vector-storage changes; the perf comparison against Boost is opt-in (GRAAF_BUILD_BOOST_PERF and GRAAF_DOWNLOAD_PERF_DATASETS, both OFF) and the web-BerkStan download points at snap-sentiment.stanford.edu rather than snap.stanford.edu (not checked here).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No siblings catalogued yet; against its own named baseline, pick Boost.Graph whenever speed matters and Graaf only when the simpler API and zero dependencies are worth a 1.1-17x slowdown.
verified_claims_summary: Graaf's own pull requests (#419, #449, #451-#456) time Graaf against Boost.Graph 1.84.0 adjacency_list<vecS, vecS, undirectedS> with Google Benchmark v1.8.2 in a Release build on SNAP web-Google and web-BerkStan with unit weights; after the September 2026 vector-storage PRs Graaf remains slower everywhere, from 1.14x (Kruskal, web-Google) to 17.01x (all-targets Dijkstra, web-BerkStan; Graaf 14.54 s vs about 0.85 s for Boost, derived from page data). No CPU, compiler version or flags beyond 'Release' are stated.
status_note: Actively developed (last commit 2026-09-28, a burst of perf PRs 2026-09-18 to 2026-09-27, several with a Claude co-author trailer) and MIT-licensed, so copyable, but the performance work is unreleased and the library is a convenience alternative to Boost.Graph, not a faster one.
